query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Systematically varying each element’s concentration in HfNbTaTiZr HEAs (by a few atomic percent around the equiatomic composition) will alter lattice distortion and phases enough to change yield strength and ductility in measurable ways, with higher Hf content generally increasing strength but also reducing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy in near-equiatomic composition.
generation.intervention: Use vacuum arc melting to produce multiple small ingots of HfNbTaTiZr with systematically altered concentrations of each principal element (e.g., ±5–10 at.% in Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr).
generation.conditions: Conduct mechanical characterization (hardness, compression or tensile tests) at room temperature (and optionally at one elevated temperature) to compare the impact of composition changes.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic size mismatch and resulting lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Shifting the fraction of each element modifies solid-solution strengthening and phase stability via changes in local ordering and lattice strains, which influences defect movement and hence mechanical behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Increasing the fraction of the larger atom (e.g., Hf) in the alloy slightly increases hardness and yield strength but may also lower ductility. Decreasing it has the opposite effect, reducing strength but improving tensile elongation.
generation.baseline: A baseline near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr ingot produced under identical melting and processing conditions for direct comparison.
generation.boundary: If any constituent is changed too drastically (beyond ~15–20 at.% from the equiatomic ratio), additional intermetallic phases may form and compromise the general high-entropy single-phase structure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact shifts in mechanical performance may depend on processing variations and minor impurities, making the magnitude of changes challenging to predict precisely.

falsification_experiment.design: Melt batches of HfNbTaTiZr alloys with controlled variations of each element (in increments of ~5–10 at.%) using vacuum arc melting to keep comparison conditions consistent. Perform mechanical tests (hardness, tensile, and/or compression tests) at ambient temperature (and an elevated temperature) to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile/compressive strength, and elongation for each variant.
measurements: Tensile or compression tests for yield and ultimate strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yield strength or ductility does not scale with composition shift (e.g., if lower Hf content unexpectedly increases yield strength), or if no detectable changes arise in either hardness or ductility after elemental adjustments, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5
